source.title: Open Questions about Ramsey-Type Statements in Reverse Mathematics

accepted.question_text: In the setting of ω-models of second-order arithmetic, does the stable Ramsey theorem for pairs with two colors imply full Ramsey's theorem for pairs with two colors, equivalently the cohesiveness principle COH?

evidence.quote: Definition 2.2 (Cohesiveness) An infinite set C is R~ -cohesive for a sequence of sets R0, R1, . . . if for each i ∈ N, C ⊆∗ Ri or C ⊆∗ Ri . ... COH is the statement “Every uniform sequence of sets R~ has an R~ -cohesive set.”

Question 2.3 Does SRT2 2 imply RT2 2 (or equivalently COH) over ω-models?
UPDATE: This question was answered negatively by Monin and Patey in [48]

accepted.question_text: Is there a natural computable instance of the stable Ramsey theorem for pairs with two colors whose every solution has non-low Turing degree, rather than the instance being artificially engineered only to avoid low solutions?
accepted.context_brief: Natural SRT^2_2 instance without low solutions

evidence.quote: Definition 2.1 (Stable Ramsey’s theorem) A function f : [N] 2 → k is stable if for every x ∈ N, lims f(x, s) exists. SRT2 k is the restriction of RT2 k to stable colorings.

Question 2.4 Is there a natural computable SRT2 2 -instance with no low solution?
Here, by “natural”, we mean an instance which carries more informational content than having no low solution.

accepted.question_text: Does every Δ0_2 set A have an infinite subset H contained either in A or in its complement such that H is itself Δ0_2 and also low2?
accepted.context_brief: Low2 Δ0_2 subsets of Δ0_2 sets

evidence.quote: Question 2.5 Does every ∆0 2 set admit an infinite subset of either it or its complement which is both low2 and ∆0 2 ?
A positive answer to Question 2.5 would enable one to build an ω-model M of SRT2 2 such that for every set X ∈ M, X is low2 and X′ is n-CEA over ∅′ .

accepted.question_text: Is there a Δ0_2 set A such that every infinite subset H contained either in A or in its complement has jump H′ of PA degree relative to ∅′?
accepted.context_brief: PA-degree jumps forced by a Δ0_2 set

evidence.quote: Question 2.6 Is there a ∆0 2 set such that every infinite subset of either it or its complement has a jump of PA degree relative to ∅′ ?
By Jockusch & Stephan [37], if some X ∈ M computes some p-cohesive set, then X′ is of PA degree relative to ∅′ .

accepted.question_text: Is there a Δ0_2 set A such that every infinite Δ0_2 subset H contained either in A or in its complement is high?

evidence.quote: Question 2.7 Is there a ∆0 2 set such that every ∆0 2 infinite subset of either it or its complement is high?
By Arslanov’s completeness criterion, a positive answer to Question 2.6 would also provide one to the following question.

accepted.question_text: Is there a coloring of the natural numbers with two colors, viewed as an instance of Ramsey's theorem for singletons RT^1_2, such that every infinite homogeneous solution H has jump H′ of PA degree relative to ∅′?

evidence.quote: Definition 1.1 (Ramsey’s theorem) A subset H of N is homogeneous for a coloring f : [N] n → k ... RTn k is the statement “Every coloring f : [N] n → k has an infinite f-homogeneous set”.
Question 2.10 Is there any RT1 2 -instance whose solutions have a jump of PA degree relative to ∅′ ?

accepted.question_text: Over ω-models, does the stable Ramsey theorem for pairs with two colors imply the sequential finite-change thin-set principle Seq*(TS^1), namely: for every uniform sequence of thin-set instances X0, X1, ..., is there a single set Y that is, up to finite changes, a solution to each instance?

evidence.quote: More formally, given some theorem P, Seq∗ (P) is the statement “For every uniform sequence of P-instances X0, X1, . . . , there is a set Y which is, up to finite changes, a solution to each of the X’s.”
Question 2.11 Does SRT2 2 imply Seq∗ (TS1 ) over ω-models?

accepted.question_text: Is there a Δ0_2 set A such that every infinite subset H contained either in A or in its complement has jump H′ of diagonally non-computable degree relative to ∅′?
accepted.context_brief: DNC-degree jumps forced by a Δ0_2 set

evidence.quote: Definition 2.9 (DNC functions) A function f : N → N is diagonally non-computable relative to X if for every e, f(e) 6= ΦX e (e).
Question 2.12 Is there a ∆0 2 set such that every infinite subset of either it or its complement has a jump of DNC degree relative to ∅′ ?

accepted.question_text: Does Ramsey-type weak König's lemma admit a universal instance, that is, a single computable RWKL instance whose every solution computes solutions to all computable RWKL instances?

evidence.quote: Definition 3.1 (Ramsey-type weak König’s lemma) ... RWKL is the statement “for every infinite subtree of 2<N, there is an infinite homogeneous set.”
Definition 3.2 (Universal instance) A computable P-instance X is universal if for every computable P-instance Y, every solution to X computes a solution to Y.
Question 3.3 Does RWKL admit a universal instance?

accepted.question_text: Is there either an instance of Ramsey's theorem for singletons with two colors, or a computable instance of Ramsey's theorem for pairs with two colors, such that every solution computes solutions to all computable instances of Ramsey-type weak König's lemma?

evidence.quote: A degree d is P-bounding relative to a degree e if every e-computable instance has a d-computable solution. The degree d is P-bounding if it is P-bounding relative to 0.
Question 3.4 Is there some instance of RT1 2 or some computable instance of RT2 2 whose solutions are RWKL-bounding?

accepted.question_text: Over RCA0, does the Ramsey-type graph-coloring principle RCOLOR2 imply Ramsey-type weak König's lemma, or at least imply the existence of a diagonally non-computable function?

evidence.quote: Definition 3.5 (Ramsey-type graph coloring) ... RCOLORk is the statement “for every infinite, locally k-colorable graph G = (V, E), there is an infinite H ⊆ V that is k-homogeneous for G.”
Question 3.6 Does RCOLOR2 imply RWKL or even DNC over RCA0?

accepted.question_text: Does the Erdős-Moser theorem admit a universal instance, that is, a single computable infinite tournament whose every infinite transitive subtournament computes solutions to all computable EM instances?

evidence.quote: Definition 4.1 (Erdős-Moser theorem) ... EM is the statement “Every infinite tournament T has an infinite transitive subtournament.”

Question 4.2 Does EM admit a universal instance?
UPDATE: This question was answered negatively by Liu and Patey in [45].

accepted.question_text: Over RCA0, does the Erdős-Moser theorem imply the cohesiveness principle COH?

evidence.quote: COH is the statement “Every uniform sequence of sets R~ has an R~ -cohesive set.”
Question 4.3 Does EM imply COH over RCA0?

accepted.question_text: Over RCA0, does the Erdős-Moser theorem imply 1-GEN, the statement that for every set X there exists a real that is 1-generic relative to X?

evidence.quote: Given an integer n ∈ N, a real is n-generic if it meets or avoids each Σ0 n set of strings. n-GEN is the statement “For every set X, there is a real n-generic relative to X”.
Question 4.5 Does EM imply 1-GEN over RCA0?

accepted.question_text: Does every computable instance of the Erdős-Moser theorem, and even every computable instance of Ramsey-type weak König's lemma, have a solution of minimal Turing degree?
accepted.context_brief: Minimal-degree solutions for EM or RWKL

evidence.quote: Question 4.6 Does every computable EM-instance (or even RWKL-instance) admit a solution of minimal degree?
Construcing a similar model of EM would answer negatively Question 4.5. The following question is a first step towards an answer.

accepted.question_text: Do the free set theorem hierarchy and, separately, the thin set theorem with infinitely many colors form strict hierarchies as the tuple size n increases?
accepted.context_brief: Strictness of FS and TS^ω hierarchies

evidence.quote: Definition 5.1 (Free set theorem) ... FSn is the statement “Every coloring f : [N] n → N has a free set”. FS is the statement (∀n) FSn.
Question 5.2 Does the free set theorem (resp. the thin set theorem with ω colors) form a strict hierarchy?

accepted.question_text: For each n at least 3, does every computable instance of the free set theorem FS^n, and likewise every computable instance of the thin set theorem TS^n, admit a low_n solution?
accepted.context_brief: Low_n solutions for FS^n and TS^n

evidence.quote: Question 5.3 For every n ≥ 3, does every computable instance of FSn (resp. TSn ) admit a lown solution?
By Cholak et al. [8], every computable instance of FS2 and TS2 admit a low2 solution. Therefore FS2 (hence TS2 ) are strictly weaker than TS3 (hence FS3 ) over RCA0.

accepted.question_text: For each n at least 3, does every Δ0_n set A have an infinite subset H contained either in A or in its complement such that H is low_n?

evidence.quote: Question 5.4 For every n ≥ 3, does every ∆0 n set admit an infinite lown subset of either it or its complement?
Non-effective instances of Ramsey’s theorem for singletons is a good starting point, since the only combinatorics involved are the pigeonhole principle.
